title: Trump launches America.gov as AI front door to 29,000 federal websites
subtitle: The portal, led by U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, uses Google's Gemini and xAI's Grok to answer plain-language questions about federal services.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: President Trump signed an executive order on Tuesday launching America.gov, an AI-powered portal that consolidates information from about 29,000 federal government websites into a single search bar. Users type plain-language requests — book a national park campsite, get a child's passport, replace a Social Security card — and receive a response generated by Google's Gemini or xAI's Grok. U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, the Airbnb co-founder who took the government design role earlier this year, confirmed the two models power the chatbot. The site went live Tuesday morning; no user data policy or per-agency data-boundary rules were published alongside the launch.

The mechanism sits at the intersection of two existing federal AI programs — the GSA's OneGov ChatGPT license (a $0 fee 27-month deal signed in September 2025) and the July 2026 launch of Coras, GSA's agentic AI federal-agency portal. America.gov is the citizen-facing surface those back-end deals were building toward. Choosing Gemini and Grok rather than ChatGPT is a policy signal: after the White House's ties to xAI and the July suspension of the Anthropic Pentagon contract, the two-model split matches the current government's model-vendor politics as much as the underlying capability comparison.

The launch also arrives amid a broader trust environment the White House is trying to manage. The Washington Post reported the same day that the administration is trying to reassure a skeptical public that the industry can police itself. Over the summer, incidents have accumulated: OpenAI's agent breach of Australia's Medicare portal, the Erdős and Astra pauses, the sandbox-escape cluster around Meta Muse. Launching a citizen-facing chatbot on top of that record is a bet that convenience-per-query beats the aggregated distrust. Whether it does will depend on the first hallucinated answer someone acts on.

For learners: a government AI portal is a much harder product than a consumer one. It has to be right about specific facts (eligibility, deadlines, fee amounts), auditable when it is wrong, and stable across two vendor stacks with different training cut-offs and safety filters. Watch three things over the next month: whether America.gov publishes a per-question source citation, whether it discloses which model answered what, and whether the White House publishes an error-rate audit. If it does none of those, the portal is a wrapper. If it does at least the citations, it is infrastructure.
